title: Order Types
hook: Know the difference before you touch a chart.

launchpad.outcome: Pick the right order type for the situation — not just recognize the names.
launchpad.missionQuestion: If price never reaches your limit price, does the order fill anyway?

markers.label: When a stop order actually triggers

slides.kicker: Market, limit, and stop orders each answer a different question
slides.title: Three order types, three jobs

items.label: Market order
items.desc: Fills immediately at whatever price is available — speed over price control.

items.label: Limit order
items.desc: Rests and only fills at your price — price control over speed.

items.label: Stop order
items.desc: Sits inactive until triggered, then acts like a market order.

right.label: Limit order
points: Waits for price to come to you

slides.body: A trader says market orders and limit orders are basically interchangeable since both "get you into a trade."

options.label: A market order prioritizes speed, a limit order prioritizes price control — that's a real trade-off, not interchangeable
options.why: Right — treating them as interchangeable ignores a real trade-off between speed and price.

options.label: Nothing — they always produce the same result
options.feedback: They don't — one chases price, the other waits for it.

slides.quote: I'll show you later which order types I personally lean on for entries. But you need to actually understand all three first — market, limit, and stop — before that preference means anything to you.

slides.kicker: Pick the order for the job
slides.body: A trader wants to protect an open long position by automatically exiting if price falls to a specific level below her entry.

options.label: A stop order
options.why: Stop orders sit inactive until triggered — exactly what a protective exit needs.

options.label: A limit order
options.feedback: A limit order rests at a price — it doesn't automatically protect a losing position past a level.

options.label: A market order
options.feedback: A market order fires the instant you place it — it can't wait to trigger only if price falls to a level.

slides.body: Price is at 100 and a trader places a limit order to buy at 98.

check.prompt: If price never trades down to 98, what happens?

options.label: The order never fills — it only fills if price actually reaches 98
options.why: A limit order only fills at your chosen price or better — no guarantee it fills at all.

options.label: It fills instantly at 100 anyway
options.feedback: That would defeat the purpose of setting a limit price in the first place.

options.label: It automatically converts to a market order after a few minutes
options.feedback: Limit orders don't auto-convert to market orders just from waiting.

slides.prompt: Imagine another AGHF member asks: "When would you actually use a stop order instead of a limit order?" How would you explain it to them?
slides.modelAnswer: A limit order is for when you want control over your entry price and are willing to risk never getting filled. A stop order is for when you need something to happen automatically once price proves a level — like a protective exit, or an entry that only makes sense once price breaks past a certain point. You reach for a stop order when you need to react to a trigger, not just wait at a price.

takeaways: Market orders trade speed for price control.
Limit orders trade price control for a guaranteed fill.
Stop orders sit inactive until price proves a level, then act like a market order.
remember: Every order type is a trade-off between speed and control.
